topic: The Carrington Event: the 1 September 1859 white-light flare, the 1–2 September geomagnetic storm, telegraphs worked on auroral current, and the July 2012 near miss
policy_note: Every narrated or on-screen fact maps to a claim. Weights: core (load-bearing) needs >=2 independent publishers incl. >=1 primary/scholarly; record (uncontested public record: dates, deaths, disclosures) needs >=2 incl. a fact-checked reference or stronger; detail needs >=2; framing needs >=1. A quote's quote_origin (first publication of the words) counts as primary evidence for that quote. Checked by reelkit/factcheck.py.

carrington1859.title: Description of a Singular Appearance seen in the Sun on September 1, 1859 (R. C. Carrington), with the Society's note of his November 1859 remarks and R. Hodgson's account
carrington1859.publisher: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, vol. 20, pp. 13–15
carrington1859.notes: Outburst 'not 15 seconds different from 11h 18m Greenwich mean time', gone by 11h 23m (5 minutes); 'two patches of intensely bright and white light broke out'; 'I hastily ran to call some one to witness the exhibition with me, and on returning within 60 seconds, was mortified to find that it was already much changed and enfeebled'; Kew: 'towards four hours after midnight there commenced a great magnetic storm'; 'he would not have it supposed that he even leans towards hastily connecting them. "One swallow does not make a summer."'

green2006.title: Eyewitness reports of the great auroral storm of 1859 (Green, Boardsen, Odenwald, Humble, Pazamickas)
green2006.notes: Two storms (28 Aug and 2 Sep); the 2 Sep storm follows the Carrington–Hodgson flare; aurora 'blood or deep crimson red', bright enough to 'read a newspaper by'; aurorae to geographic latitudes of 25° and lower; Boston–Portland line 'worked for about two hours without the usual batteries on the auroral current'; collects the AJS (Loomis/editors 1859–1861) reports.

nasa2008.title: A Super Solar Flare (Trudy E. Bell, Tony Phillips)
nasa2008.notes: Syndicated text of the NASA feature. 11:18 AM, Thursday 1 Sept 1859, 33-year-old Carrington in his private observatory projecting an 11-inch image; 'Spark discharges shocked telegraph operators and set the telegraph paper on fire. Even when telegraphers disconnected the batteries powering the lines, aurora-induced electric currents in the wires still allowed messages to be transmitted.'

nasa2014.title: Near Miss: The Solar Superstorm of July 2012
nasa2014.notes: CME tore through Earth orbit on 23 July 2012 and hit STEREO-A; Baker: 'If the eruption had occurred only one week earlier, Earth would have been in the line of fire'; 'the July 2012 storm was in all respects at least as strong as the 1859 Carrington event ... The only difference is, it missed'; Carrington storms 'ignited Northern Lights as far south as Cuba and caused global telegraph lines to spark, setting fire to some telegraph offices'; NAS: impact could exceed $2 trillion; Riley 2014: 12% chance per decade.

baker2013.title: A major solar eruptive event in July 2012: Defining extreme space weather scenarios (Baker et al.)
baker2013.notes: 'Our advanced technological society was very fortunate, indeed, that the solar storm did not occur just a week or so earlier'; would have rivalled the Carrington storm (Dst up to about −1200 nT). Quoted in Reuters (Kemp, 25 Jul 2014).

reuters2014.title: Time to be afraid – preparing for the next big solar storm (John Kemp)
reuters2014.notes: Quotes Baker et al. 2013 ('just a week or so earlier ... Earth would have been directly targeted'); STEREO-A was hit; Carrington Dst ≈ −850 nT, 1989 Quebec −589 nT.

ars2012.title: 1859's 'Great Auroral Storm' — the week the Sun touched the earth (Matthew Lasar)
ars2012.notes: Full Boston–Portland transcript ('Mine is disconnected, and we are working with the auroral current. How do you receive my writing?' / 'Better than with our batteries on.'); Rocky Mountain News correspondent: 'We were high up on the Rocky Mountains sleeping in the open air ... A little after midnight we were awakened by the auroral light, so bright that one could easily read common print' — some of the party began making breakfast thinking dawn had come; Washington Daily National Intelligencer: 'worked for about two hours without the usual batteries'.

history2025.title: A Perfect Solar Superstorm: The 1859 Carrington Event
history2025.notes: Sparks showering from telegraph machines, shocking operators and setting papers ablaze; 2 Sept: Boston office could transmit to Portland, Maine with batteries unplugged, using only the auroral current.

armagh.title: Carrington Event (adapted from M. Infield)
armagh.notes: First flare recorded; independently observed by Carrington and Hodgson; New York Times (via Green et al. 2006) on Boston–Portland communication with batteries disconnected.

scienceblog2026.title: In 1859 the Carrington storm shocked telegraph operators and pushed auroras to Cuba; a repeat today could disrupt grids, satellites, radio and navigation, but it would not simply switch off every electronic device
scienceblog2026.notes: 'Roughly 17 hours later, Earth's magnetic field convulsed'; auroras reached Cuba and Hawaii; Boston–Portland batteries disconnected (AJS); a repeat would not 'simply switch off every electronic device'.

colombia2015.title: The Grand Aurorae Borealis Seen in Colombia in 1859 (Moreno Cárdenas et al.)
colombia2015.notes: Quotes Carrington (1863): 'Mr. Hodgson at Highgate and I at Redhill witnessed and described a singular outbreak of light'; outburst at 11:18 UT.

claims.text: During the September 1859 storm, operators on the Boston–Portland telegraph line disconnected their batteries and kept working the line on the auroral (storm-induced) current, for about two hours.
vo: two telegraph operators unplugged their batteries and kept on talking
disconnected their batteries
for about two hours on the aurora's current alone

claims.text: The current that worked the line was induced by the geomagnetic storm (popularly: it came from the sky).
vo: the power was coming from the sky
claims.caveat: Physically: a rapidly changing geomagnetic field induced currents in long grounded wires; the aurora is a symptom, not a power source. Myth M02 is avoided by never calling it free power.

claims.text: On 1 September 1859 at about 11:18 Greenwich mean time, Richard Carrington, sketching sunspots at his private observatory at Redhill, saw two patches of intensely bright white light break out over a large sunspot group.
vo: on september 1st at 11 18 in the morning the astronomer richard carrington was sketching sunspots
two patches of intensely bright white light broke out

claims.text: Carrington's observatory was at Redhill, Surrey, south of London.
claims.caveat: armagh does not name Redhill explicitly; colombia2015 quotes Carrington (1863) 'I at Redhill'; the 1857 engraving on Wikimedia Commons is titled Carrington's house and observatory, Redhill.

claims.text: Carrington ran to call a witness; returning within 60 seconds he found the outburst already much changed and enfeebled; it vanished by 11:23, five minutes after it began.
vo: he ran to find a witness
within sixty seconds it was fading
five minutes and it was gone

claims.text: About seventeen hours after the flare (towards four hours after midnight, per the Kew magnetographs), a great magnetic storm began.
vo: about seventeen hours later earth's magnetic field began to shake
claims.caveat: Modern reconstructions give ~17.6 h Sun–Earth transit for the CME; Carrington's note gives the storm onset 'towards four hours after midnight' (about 16.5–17.5 h after 11:18).

claims.text: Aurorae of the September storm were deep crimson red and were seen at very low latitudes, as far south as Cuba.
vo: the night sky turned blood red as far south as cuba
screen: AURORA SEEN AS FAR SOUTH AS CUBA

claims.text: A Rocky Mountain News correspondent sleeping in the open air in the Rocky Mountains was woken a little after midnight by aurora bright enough to read print; some of the party began making breakfast, believing it was morning.
vo: in the rocky mountains campers woke after midnight and some started making breakfast
they thought it was dawn
claims.caveat: Popular retellings say 'gold miners'; the original letter only says a party sleeping in the open air (myth M01).

claims.text: Telegraph systems were disrupted: sparks jumped from equipment, operators received shocks and telegraph paper caught fire.
vo: sparks jumped from the equipment operators took shocks and telegraph paper caught fire

claims.text: Many telegraph lines were unusable for 8 hours or more.
claims.caveat: Green et al.: 'many of which were unusable for 8 h or more'; History.com: Boston office could not transmit from 8 a.m.

claims.text: Carrington reported the flare and the magnetic storm but would not have it supposed that he leaned towards connecting them: 'One swallow does not make a summer.'
claims.quote: One swallow does not make a summer.
vo: carrington had seen the flare and the storm
but he wouldn't claim they were connected
one swallow he said does not make a summer
screen: “One swallow does not make a summer.”
R. C. CARRINGTON · ROYAL ASTRONOMICAL SOCIETY · NOV. 1859

claims.text: On 23 July 2012 a coronal mass ejection at least as strong as the Carrington storm (Baker) crossed Earth's orbit and hit STEREO-A; had it erupted about one week earlier, Earth would have been in the line of fire.
vo: in july 2012 a storm at least as strong crossed earth's orbit
one week earlier and it would have hit us
claims.caveat: 'At least as strong' is Baker's assessment (NASA 2014); Baker et al. 2013 put the would-be Dst near −1200 nT, comparable to Carrington estimates (−800 to −1750 nT).

claims.text: A Carrington-class storm will recur; today it would meet a society dependent on electrical networks (NAS: impact could exceed $2 trillion; Riley: ~12% per decade).
vo: next time it will find a world built on wires
claims.caveat: Effects would be serious but uneven: grids, satellites, radio, navigation — not 'every device switches off' (scienceblog2026).

claims.text: In 1859 the storm's current worked a telegraph line.
vo: in 1859 the sky ran a telegraph line

claims.text: Boston operator to Portland during the storm: 'Mine is disconnected, and we are working with the auroral current.'
claims.quote: Mine is disconnected, and we are working with the auroral current.
screen: “MINE IS DISCONNECTED, AND WE ARE WORKING WITH THE AURORAL CURRENT.”
claims.caveat: Transcript first printed in the Boston Traveller (2 Sept 1859) and reprinted in the American Journal of Science; quote_origin points to the scholarly compilation that reproduces it.

myths.myth: Gold miners in the Rockies got up and made breakfast.
myths.reality: The Rocky Mountain News letter describes a party sleeping in the open air in the mountains; 'gold miners' is a later embellishment.

myths.myth: Telegraphs ran on free power from the aurora.
myths.reality: The storm induced unstable currents in long grounded wires; on some lines operators could work without batteries for a while, while elsewhere lines failed.

myths.myth: A Carrington event today would instantly switch off every electronic device.
myths.reality: Serious, uneven effects on grids, satellites, radio and navigation; not a universal off switch.

guardrails.why: Embellishment; the original source says a party sleeping in the open air (myth M01).
Frederic Royce's shock was reported for the earlier 28–29 August storm, not this one.
It is the first flare recorded, not the first to happen.

landscape.our_gap: Start from the human moment (two operators talking with their batteries unplugged) instead of doom; let the primary sources speak (Carrington's own 'one swallow' caution, the telegraph transcript), correct the 'gold miners' myth on screen, and land on the 2012 near miss with sourced numbers instead of apocalypse claims.
